YOUR PRESENT PERFECT SEA CHART
FORM · HAVE / HAS + PAST PARTICIPLE
I HAVE BEEN out and back. Quinn HAS GONE and is away.
NEGATIVE · HASN'T / HAVEN'T + PARTICIPLE
The fog HASN'T lifted, so the crews HAVEN'T slept.
EVER / NEVER · ANY TIME UNTIL NOW
HAVE you EVER been out there? I HAVE NEVER liked deep water.
JUST · ALREADY · YET
Hoy HAS JUST arrived. Baird HAS ALREADY refused and HASN'T signed YET.
SINCE + A POINT IN TIME · FOR + A PERIOD
The boats HAVE been missing SINCE dawn, FOR eight hours.
A finished time takes the PAST SIMPLE: the boat WENT out at six. TODAY and THIS WEEK are not finished.
GO DOWN TO THE PIER
CHAPTER 1 · KILMARA
A BOAT COMES BACK
Dawn on the pier. A creel boat turns in the bay with its rope trailing. The seats are empty.
The yellow barrel in the stern hangs by a stub of rope. Both coats are aboard.
What do you say to the men on the pier?
Present Perfect for a past event with a result now: HAS + TAKEN. TOOK is Past Simple, and one sea takes HAS.
ONE BERTH STAYS EMPTY
You ring the harbour bell. Doors open along the street. Men count the boats at the pier, then count them again.
The brass bell rings over one empty space, and no engine answers from the Sound.
What do you say when the ringing stops?
The negative of the Present Perfect is HAVE NOT + COME. English never builds it with BE, and THEY takes HAVE.
THE PROVOST SAYS NO
Provost Baird will not close the water. Regatta Week starts tomorrow, and the whole village needs the money.
The red buoy stays out in the Sound, and no coastguard boat is in the bay.
How do you ask Baird about the coastguard?
A yes/no question puts HAVE first: HAVE + YOU + CALLED. HAVE always needs the participle, never CALL or CALLING.
THE WOMAN FROM OBAN
A car stops at the top of the slip. Dr. Maren Hoy carries a metal case down.
The sonar case is new and unscratched, and she is younger than you expected.
What do you ask Dr. Hoy first?
EVER asks about any time up to now, and it sits between the subject and the participle: HAVE + YOU + EVER + DIVED.
THE RING OF HORN
Dr. Hoy holds a jar up to the lamp. Inside is a black ring of horn, cut from something's beak.
The black ring in the glass jar is heavier than it looks in her hand.
What does Dr. Hoy say about the ring?
NEVER already means not at any time, so HAVE stays positive: HAVE NEVER + HELD. HOLD is irregular and its participle is HELD.
QUINN OPENS HIS SHED
Angus Quinn opens his shed. Yellow marker barrels hang along the wall. He turns one round, and you lift your radio.
The yellow barrel on the wall is bitten clean through the middle, and still swinging.
What do you say into the radio?
JUST means a moment ago and goes between HAS and the participle: HAS + JUST + FOUND. It cannot sit at the end.
CHAPTER 2 · THE REEF
SHAPES ON THE SCREEN
Hoy swings her sonar float over the reef. Quinn cuts the engine. Shapes crowd the screen at once.
The orange sonar float is barely wet, and the screen is full of moving shapes.
Hoy ___ the shapes on her sonar screen.
ALREADY goes between HAS and MARKED. HAS needs the participle MARKED, and one person takes HAS, not HAVE.
CHAPTER 2 · THE SEA CAVES
THE MOUTH AT LOW WATER
You and Hoy take the inflatable under the headland at low water. The roof drops to a hand above you.
The storm lantern shows wet oar marks on the rock, and Quinn's boat is gone.
Quinn ___ into the cave ahead of you.
ALREADY sits between HAS and the participle ROWED. HAS never takes the bare ROW, and one man takes HAS.
CUT EDGE TO EDGE
Hoy pulls a creel net over the rail. It is cut through, edge to edge. Quinn turns it over.
The torn net hangs on the rail. Quinn holds an end and looks at the water.
Quinn ___ about the net yet.
YET needs the Present Perfect negative: HAS NOT + SPOKEN. The Past Simple cannot take YET, and SPOKE is not the participle.
THE EMPTY DINGHY
Deep in the caves a dinghy lies over against the wall, half swamped. Water slaps the bare boards.
The dinghy lamp burns on its hook, and both oars are still aboard.
The man who owns this dinghy ___ yet.
YET goes with the Present Perfect negative: HAS NOT + TURNED UP. DID and WAS cannot carry a participle here.
ONE SEAL LEFT
Quinn takes the Selkie past the low rocks. One seal on the whole rock. Hoy counts twice, then lowers the binoculars.
The last seal lies alone on the rock, and Hoy's count comes to one.
The rest of the colony has been gone ___.
SINCE gives the point where it started: SINCE Monday morning. FOR needs a length of time, and ON cannot follow a Present Perfect.
SHELLS ON THE LEDGE
The passage opens into a chamber. Hoy lowers her sonar into the pool. The floor drops away under it.
The broken creel on the ledge is Quinn's. He lost it on Tuesday, in calm water.
The broken creel up on the ledge ___.
SINCE gives the day it started: SINCE Tuesday. English needs HAS BEEN here, never IS here and never IS BEING here.
SOMETHING TOUCHES THE HULL
Something long drags down the side of the Selkie and is gone. Quinn turns the wheel towards the old wreck.
The scarred hull plate is still wet, and Quinn knows the noise without looking.
What does Quinn say about his years here?
FOR measures a length of time reaching now: HAVE + FISHED + FOR forty years. The present continuous cannot reach back.
THE CAVE IS FILLING
The cave is filling fast. Quinn is aboard the inflatable again, wet through. The mouth is still ahead of you.
The wet tide line is over your head now, and your watch reads two hours.
What do you say about the time?
FOR measures a length of time up to now: FOR two hours. SINCE needs a starting point, and AGO forces the Past Simple.
CHAPTER 3 · THE WRECK
FOUR METRES OF WATER
The Selkie stops over the Morag in four metres of water. Hoy goes over the side with a mask and comes up again.
A yellow barrel rises out of the wreck, and Hoy is back at the ladder.
Hoy ___ down to the wreck.
BEEN is there and back; GONE is still away. Hoy is at the ladder, so HAS BEEN. WENT is Past Simple, not the participle.
THE SCAR ON HIS ARM
Quinn rolls his sleeve back. The scar runs from wrist to elbow. He says the village laughed at him once.
The old harpoon head in his hand is pitted and bent out of true.
How do you ask about the scar on his arm?
HOW LONG asks about time up to now and inverts the auxiliary: HAVE + YOU + KNOWN. DO is never the auxiliary here.
TWENTY-EIGHT YEARS DOWN
Quinn points down at the wreck. Twenty-eight years on the bottom, he says, and the village still will not say her name.
The brass porthole is scoured bright, and the hull plates below it are split open.
The Morag ___ in 1998.
A finished time forces the Past Simple: SANK in 1998. The Present Perfect never says WHEN, and the participle is SUNK.
CHAPTER 4 · THE CORRY
A TURN ROUND THE DRUM
Quinn takes a turn round the iron drum. The Selkie leans over. Hoy braces herself against the wheelhouse door.
Smoke comes off the rope round the iron drum, and something below is taking it.
What does Quinn say about the rope?
One rope takes HAS: THE ROPE + HAS + GONE. HAVE goes with plural subjects, and WENT is Past Simple, not the participle.
CHAPTER 4 · THE NIGHT WATCH
THE LIGHTS ON THE WATER
The regatta lights burn over the moored boats. Nothing moves on the water. You walk the quay end to end.
The harbour lamp shows a line of moored boats. The decks are all dark and bare.
Every skipper in the harbour ___.
EVERY with a singular noun takes HAS: EVERY SKIPPER + HAS + COME. CAME is Past Simple, not the participle.
IT COMES UP
An arm comes up out of the sea and lies over the side. The rail bends under it. Hoy does not move.
The arm over the side is thicker than a man and pale in the lamplight.
Quinn says it is the first time anyone ___.
After IT IS THE FIRST TIME English takes the Present Perfect: HAS + TOUCHED. HAD belongs to a past frame.
ONE LAMP STILL BURNING
One boat after another goes dark along the pontoon. Somewhere a halyard knocks. You count the lights down to one.
The last lit lamp on the water is a masthead light, small and white.
Quinn says it is the first time the harbour ___ this dark.
IT IS THE FIRST TIME takes the Present Perfect: HAS + BEEN. HAD belongs to a past frame, and HARBOUR is singular.
THE ENGINE STOPS
Quinn goes down to the engine. The Selkie loses way, and the Corry takes her round again.
The engine lamp swings over the hot block, and the deck is wet to the plates.
Which question do you ask about the engine tonight?
TONIGHT is not finished, so the Present Perfect counts it: HAS + IT + STOPPED. DID belongs to a finished time.
THE PONTOON LIFTS
The pontoon lifts under your feet and drops back. Ropes come up out of the water hard and tight.
The mooring rope runs from a bent steel cleat straight down into black water.
Which question do you ask Quinn tonight?
A count that stands now takes the Present Perfect: HAVE + YOU + LOST. DID needs the bare verb, and the question must invert.
CHAPTER 5 · THE LAST RUN
THE THIRD ONE GOES
Hoy swings the third barrel up onto the rail. The rope runs out behind it. Quinn holds the Selkie into the sea.
The sun is still high, and two yellow barrels ride in the wake.
Hoy has thrown two barrels over the side ___.
THIS MORNING is not finished, so the Present Perfect fits. AT SIX is a finished point, and AGO always takes the Past Simple.
THE LINE GOES SLACK
The line goes out and the drum screams. Quinn holds the wheel. The fourth barrel goes under and stays under.
The harpoon line runs off the drum and stands out hard across the water.
What do you say into the radio at last?
The result stands now, so the Present Perfect: HAS + GOT. BE never carries a participle, and KILMARA is singular.
